prompt.context: Marble Front Supplies is a producer of kitchen appliances and kitchen supplies. Marble Front is a strong brand, and historically the company had significant advertising and marketing expenses to maintain their brand. In the past, growth has been steady, driven by a combination of product line extensions and key acquisitions of specialty item producers. Sales go through a number of channels, including superstores, which are increasingly critical. These superstores have gained considerable share in the past few years, and constantly pressure us to lower our margins as they substitute generic products for traditional brand names like Marble Front. Recent drops in sales and profits have made Marble Front an acquisition target.
prompt.question: Our client is a private equity firm considering purchasing Marble Front. The client wants us to do due diligence on Marble Front's production facilities, and wants us to size the opportunity for production efficiencies. They believe Marble Front needs to lower costs to stay competitive in this market. What are the factors we should examine to determine whether Marble Front can lower production costs?

clarifying_info.q: What are Marble Front's current revenues?
clarifying_info.a: Current production generates $475 million in revenues.

clarifying_info.q: How many factories does Marble Front operate and where?
clarifying_info.a: The client currently produces SKUs in 3 factories located in Michigan, Mexico, and New Jersey.

clarifying_info.q: What is the annual production and capacity for each factory?
clarifying_info.a: Michigan: 5,000 SKUs produced / 8,500 SKUs capacity. Mexico: 4,500 SKUs produced / 12,000 SKUs capacity. New Jersey: 3,000 SKUs produced / 5,500 SKUs capacity.

clarifying_info.q: What are the cost details for each factory?

exhibits.title: Factory Production and Capacity
exhibits.shows: A table showing annual production (SKUs) and annual capacity (SKUs) for each of the three factories: Michigan, Mexico, and New Jersey.
exhibits.data: Michigan: 5,000 SKUs produced, 8,500 SKUs capacity. Mexico: 4,500 SKUs produced, 12,000 SKUs capacity. New Jersey: 3,000 SKUs produced, 5,500 SKUs capacity.

exhibits.title: Factory Fixed and Variable Costs
exhibits.shows: A table or chart showing fixed costs and variable costs per SKU for each of the three factories: Michigan, Mexico, and New Jersey.
exhibits.data: Michigan: variable cost $7,900/SKU, fixed cost $15M/year. Mexico: variable cost $4,000/SKU, fixed cost $18M/year. New Jersey: variable cost $8,500/SKU, fixed cost $20M/year.

framework: Capacity utilization: calculate current utilization across all three plants and identify slack
Cost structure: analyze fixed vs. variable costs per plant to find highest-cost facilities
Consolidation scenarios: evaluate combinations of plants (move production to lower-cost facilities)
Financial impact: quantify total cost savings and any revenue impact for each scenario
Implementation considerations: closing costs, union contracts, capital leases, hiring, timelines
Strategic risks: public backlash from offshoring, loss of excess capacity for future demand growth

questions.prompt: What is the current total production, total capacity, and capacity utilization across all three plants?
questions.guidance: Candidate should sum production and capacity across all three plants, then divide to get utilization. Should note utilization is low (~48%), signaling room for consolidation.

math.setup: Total production = Michigan + Mexico + New Jersey. Total capacity = Michigan + Mexico + New Jersey. Utilization = Total production / Total capacity.
math.answer: ~48% utilization, meaning roughly half of total capacity sits idle.

questions.prompt: What are the possible consolidation scenarios, and what is the current total annual cost across all three plants?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify three logical scenarios: (1) move NJ into Michigan, (2a) move Michigan into Mexico, (2b) move NJ into Mexico, (3) move both Michigan and NJ into Mexico. Should also calculate baseline total cost.

math.setup: Total cost per plant = Fixed cost + (Production × Variable cost per SKU). Sum across all plants for total.
math.answer: $136M total annual cost across three plants.

questions.prompt: Scenario 1: How much would Marble Front save by combining New Jersey production into Michigan?
questions.guidance: Candidate eliminates NJ fixed costs and gains variable cost savings on NJ's 3,000 SKUs (lower VC in Michigan vs NJ). Michigan still has sufficient capacity (8,500 - 5,000 = 3,500 spare).

math.setup: Savings = NJ fixed costs eliminated + (NJ production × variable cost reduction per SKU). Variable cost reduction = NJ VC - Michigan VC.
steps: Variable cost savings on NJ production = 3,000 × $600 = $1.8M

questions.prompt: Scenario 2a: How much would Marble Front save by combining Michigan production into Mexico?
questions.guidance: Candidate eliminates Michigan fixed costs and gains variable cost savings on Michigan's 5,000 SKUs (much lower VC in Mexico vs Michigan). Mexico has sufficient spare capacity (12,000 - 4,500 = 7,500 spare).

math.setup: Savings = Michigan fixed costs eliminated + (Michigan production × variable cost reduction per SKU). Variable cost reduction = Michigan VC - Mexico VC.
steps: Variable cost savings on Michigan production = 5,000 × $3,900 = $19.5M

questions.prompt: Scenario 2b: How much would Marble Front save by combining New Jersey production into Mexico?
questions.guidance: Candidate eliminates NJ fixed costs and gains variable cost savings on NJ's 3,000 SKUs (much lower VC in Mexico vs NJ).

math.setup: Savings = NJ fixed costs eliminated + (NJ production × variable cost reduction per SKU). Variable cost reduction = NJ VC - Mexico VC.
steps: Variable cost savings on NJ production = 3,000 × $4,500 = $13.5M

questions.prompt: Scenario 3: How much would Marble Front save by combining both Michigan and New Jersey into Mexico, reducing total production to 12,000 SKUs (Mexico's full capacity)?
questions.guidance: Candidate must account for the cost savings from running only Mexico, but also the revenue loss from producing 500 fewer SKUs (12,500 → 12,000). Net savings = cost savings minus revenue loss.

math.setup: New total cost = Mexico fixed + (12,000 × Mexico variable). Revenue loss = (production decrease / original production) × total revenues. Net savings = (original total cost - new total cost) - revenue loss.
math.answer: ~$49-51M net annual savings (after revenue loss from 500 fewer SKUs produced).

questions.prompt: What other costs or revenues should we consider when sizing the opportunity for production consolidation?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify implementation costs and one-time charges that offset annual savings.

questions.prompt: How high would per-plant closing costs need to be before Scenario 3 is no longer the best option compared to Scenario 2a? What other disadvantages does Scenario 3 have?
questions.guidance: The incremental benefit of Scenario 3 over Scenario 2a is $49M - $34.5M = $14.5M. Candidate should recognize that if closing two plants costs more than $14.5M in total (one-time), Scenario 3's advantage disappears. Per-plant threshold mentioned in casebook is ~$16.5M (comparing marginal costs of closing NJ on top of 2a). Also flag that Scenario 3 uses 100% of Mexico capacity, eliminating flexibility for demand growth.

math.setup: Incremental annual benefit of Scenario 3 vs 2a = $49M - $34.5M. One-time closing costs to break even.
steps: If per-plant closing costs exceed ~$16.5M, Scenario 2a becomes more profitable than Scenario 3 on a marginal basis
math.answer: Per-plant closing costs above ~$16.5M would make Scenario 2a preferable; Scenario 3 also eliminates expansion flexibility.

brainstorming.prompt: What other costs or revenues might we consider when sizing the opportunity for production consolidation?

categories.name: One-time closing costs
ideas: Buyout of union contracts in Michigan and New Jersey
Losses on capital leases for plant equipment or real estate
Severance and HR costs for displaced workers

categories.name: Expansion costs in Mexico
ideas: Hiring and training costs for new workers in Mexico
Capital investment to expand Mexico plant capacity if needed

categories.name: Revenue and operational risks
ideas: Production disruption during transition reducing revenues
Quality control risks during ramp-up at Mexico plant
Lead time and supply chain complexity from single location

categories.name: Reputational and political risks
ideas: Public backlash from outsourcing manufacturing jobs to Mexico
Brand risk if customers perceive lower-quality manufacturing

categories.name: Strategic considerations
ideas: No remaining excess capacity for unexpected demand growth
Ability to serve US customers quickly from a Mexico-only footprint

recommendation: Recommend Scenario 3: consolidate both Michigan and New Jersey production into Mexico, yielding approximately $49M in net annual savings after accounting for lost revenues from the 500-SKU production reduction
This is the highest-value scenario among all options analyzed ($49M vs. $34.5M for Scenario 2a, $33.5M for Scenario 2b, and $21.8M for Scenario 1)
risks: Using 100% of Mexico's capacity eliminates flexibility for unexpected demand growth or future expansion
If per-plant closing costs exceed approximately $16.5M, Scenario 2a (Michigan into Mexico, $34.5M savings) becomes more attractive on a marginal cost basis
Public backlash from shifting manufacturing jobs out of the US (Michigan and New Jersey closures)
next_steps: Quantify one-time implementation costs: union contract buyouts, capital lease terminations, severance, and Mexico plant expansion capex
Assess demand outlook to determine probability of needing capacity beyond 12,000 SKUs
Evaluate labor and regulatory environment in Mexico for expanded operations
Define transition timeline to minimize production disruption and revenue impact
